_comment: Rules for tools/licence-scan.py (copied, MPL-2.0; see THIRD_PARTY.md). Every list stays short and every exemption gives its reason (the scanner refuses to load one without). The allow-list is this repository's licence policy: widening it is a maintainer decision, not a contributor's. This repository is MIT (LICENSE).

wording.why: GNU GPL, LGPL or AGPL licence text: copyleft, not on the allow-list
GNU LGPL licence text: copyleft, not on the allow-list
GNU AGPL: network copyleft, not on the allow-list
the Free Software Foundation, named by GPL-family headers
a licence identifier that is not on the allow-list
'All rights reserved' in a header: no permission to copy
a Stack Exchange answer: CC BY-SA, not on the allow-list for code

provenance.why: glibc is LGPL-2.1: its code may not be copied or ported
the IBM 'Ultimate Solution' routines in glibc, LGPL-2.1

permissions._comment: Code used by its author's permission with no open-source licence. A register row says `PERMISSION <name>`; each name says where the permission is recorded. None is recorded; adding one is the maintainer's decision.

scoped._comment: Licences allowed for named files only, never as a general code licence: licence id -> {aliases, globs, why}. A register row or SPDX id passes only when every file it covers matches the globs. Adding one is the maintainer's decision.

CC-BY-4.0.why: assets only (images, sounds, models, structures), never code

exempt.why: the scanner names the rules it enforces
the register names each third-party licence
writes and checks the SPDX headers of the files the scaffolders copy (VENDORED.tsv), so it names the identifiers it writes
port-fork's licence stage: it reads a fork's licence file and names each licence it can recognise, copyleft ones included, to decide whether a public fork may go ahead
publish-port: writes a fork's own licence (whatever its authors chose) onto the pages it generates
publish-port's tests: forks under different licences
publish-port's generated pages, which name the fork's licence
the publish-port skill: how a fork's licence and its authors' permission decide what may be published
